We can find the variance using the same process we used to find the mean or expected value.

On the board the two integrals are boxed; the first box has the label “” written above it with an arrow, the second has an arrow to “1”.

✎ Explanation (added)

Where the first line comes from. For a discrete variable (Lecture 8) : each squared distance from the mean, weighted by its probability. Cut the line into small pieces of width and pick a point in each piece; the probability of a piece is about . Adding up and letting turns the sum into the integral, exactly as Lecture 11 did for .

Why the shortcut works. Expanding gives three integrals. The middle one is , so it contributes ; the last is the total area 1, so it contributes . This is the same algebra as the board with , , . In practice the shortcut is easier: you integrate once instead of expanding inside the integral.

The standard deviation is , in the same units as .

5Mean, median, quartiles and percentiles

Comments:

The expected value or mean is still a measure of center in the sense where you ask “where should you place a fulcrum so things balance”.

The median is still a measure of center where you find the value so half the area under the curve lies to left of and half lies to the right.

The “… above. (… course).” at the left edge of image 8 is the end of the previous board, on the next panel.

Similarly for quartiles and percentiles.

If is the first quartile (or 25th percentile),

✎ Explanation (added)

Same words as Lectures 2 and 3, new meaning. With data, the median and quartiles came from a sorted list. For a density they come from area: the median is where the cdf reaches 0.5, , and is where it reaches 0.25. In general the th percentile is the value with area to its left.

The uniform example. On , gives , the same as the mean, because the density is symmetric. gives , and .

The picture above. For on the cdf is . Solving gives ; solving gives . The mean is . The mean sits to the right of the median, as it did for right-skewed data in Lecture 2.

Textbook · §4.2, p. 151: the th percentile is defined by (Expression 4.2, Figure 4.10). p. 152: the median of a continuous distribution is the 50th percentile, written (Devore keeps for the median of a sample); Figure 4.12 shows that a symmetric density has its median at the centre. Example 4.9 (pp. 151–152) finds a median of .347 by solving a cubic. The fulcrum picture is not in §4.2.

9Finding areas: the table

How do we find the area under a section of the normal curve?

The pdf does not have an antiderivative that can be expressed in terms of elementary functions.

Method 1: Numerical integration. ✗

Method 2: Use table or technology. ✓

The “?.” at the right edge of image 16 is a leftover mark; it is in the same spot in images 19, 20 and 22.

✎ Explanation (added)

“No elementary antiderivative” means there is no formula built from powers, exponentials, logs and trig functions whose derivative is . The areas still exist; they have to be computed numerically. The table is a list of those computed areas, , for to two decimal places, so we never integrate by hand.

Textbook · §4.3, p. 158: “None of the standard integration techniques can be used”, so the areas were computed numerically and tabulated.

-scores just tell you how many standard deviations away from the mean a value is.

example:

  • A -score of −1.8 means the value is 1.8 standard deviations below the mean.

13Example: sugar packets

Example

Example  A factory manufactures 2 gram packets of sugar.

The weights of sugar in the packages are normally distributed with a mean of 2.0 grams and a standard deviation of 0.2 grams.

What fraction of sugar packets produced contain between 1.75 and 2.25 grams of sugar.

The “1” of 1.75 is written over a scribble.

Let measure the weight of sugar in a packet.

The question written again lower on this board (“What fraction of sugar packets produced contain between 1.75 and 2.25 grams of sugar.”) is the same board as image 29, photographed again after the top was erased.

✎ Explanation (added)

The numbers. and : both limits are 1.25 standard deviations from the mean. Row 1.2, column .05 of the table is .8944; row −1.2, column .05 is .1056 (and by symmetry). So : about 78.9% of packets contain between 1.75 and 2.25 g.

The board writes so it is clear the second number is the variance, as in section 7.

TI-84: normalcdf(1.75, 2.25, 2, 0.2) = 0.78870 ≈ .7887. Enter σ = 0.2, not the variance 0.04. The calculator's .7887 differs from the board's .7888 only because each table entry is rounded to four decimals (.894350 − .105650 = .788700).

Try it · standardizing
Change the mean and standard deviation. The curve is redrawn over μ ± 3.5σ every time, so its shape never changes; only the numbers on the grams ruler move. Then drag the interval and watch the -scores.
From the table
Exact (calculator)

Try μ = 2.0, σ = 0.2, then double σ to 0.4: the same interval 1.75–2.25 now covers only ±0.63 standard deviations and the fraction drops to about 0.47.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • A pdf on an interval (uniform, or a polynomial like ) is given: find , , with the shortcut, and the standard deviation; sometimes .
  • Find the median or a quartile of a continuous distribution by setting the area to the left equal to 0.5 or 0.25 and solving.
  • Standard normal probabilities from the table, with a sketch: , , .
  • Use the table in reverse: the critical value or -value that leaves a given area in a tail (e.g. .0250 gives ±1.96).
  • A word problem with : define , standardize both ends, look up and subtract, and state the answer as a fraction or percentage, with the second parameter read correctly as variance or standard deviation.
